title: How to Stop Thinking About Your Ex: 14 Ways That Work
h1: How to Stop Thinking About Your Ex: 14 Ways to Quiet the Replay Loop
description: Can't get them out of your head? Learn how to stop thinking about your ex with 14 practical ways to process the pain, cut reminders and focus on your future.
keyword: how to stop thinking about your ex
excerpt: Stuck replaying the relationship? These 14 practical steps help you process the pain, break the rumination loop and look forward again.
intro:
You are fine at work, fine with friends, and then a song comes on or you pass that coffee shop, and suddenly you are back in the relationship, replaying the last fight or the best weekend. Thinking about an ex after a breakup is completely normal. Thinking about them constantly, weeks or months later, is exhausting.

This guide focuses on the mental side of moving on: why your brain keeps looping, and 14 practical ways to process the pain, interrupt rumination, remove reminders and gradually point your attention toward your own future. You will not forget them overnight, but you can absolutely stop letting them run your thoughts.
body:
Why you can't stop thinking about your ex

A relationship weaves itself into your routines, plans and sense of who you are. When it ends, your brain keeps reaching for the familiar connection, a bit like reaching for a light switch in a room that has been rearranged. Unanswered questions (“Why did it end?” “What if I'd done something differently?”) also keep the mind looping, because it is trying to solve a problem that may not have a satisfying answer.

Understanding this helps you be gentler with yourself. You are not weak or obsessed. You are adjusting, and you can help that adjustment along.

Get past the initial pain

1. Talk to someone you trust

Thoughts that stay inside tend to grow. Saying them out loud to a friend, sibling or mentor often shrinks them back to normal size. Choose someone who will listen without either trashing your ex or pushing you to get back together.

2. Let go of the anger

Anger can feel protective, but replaying what they did wrong keeps them at the center of your mind. Write an unsendable letter that says everything, then tear it up or delete it. The goal is release, not a verdict.

3. Be honest with yourself about what happened

Nostalgia edits out the bad parts. Write a balanced account of the relationship: what was good, what was not and why it ended. When your brain serves up the highlight reel, you will have the full story to compare it to.

4. Get the help you need

If you are struggling to sleep, eat, work or find joy weeks after the breakup, talking with a licensed therapist is a strong, practical move. Breakups sometimes stir up older wounds, and support helps you work through them faster.

Break the rumination loop

5. Notice the thought, then redirect it

When a thought about your ex appears, name it: “There's that memory again.” Then deliberately move your attention to something concrete, like a task, a conversation or your breathing. You are not trying to suppress the thought, which tends to backfire; you are practicing not following it.

6. Set a daily “ex time” limit

It sounds odd, but it works for many people. Give yourself 15 minutes a day to think, journal or cry about the breakup. When thoughts pop up outside that window, tell yourself, “Not now; later.” Containing the thoughts makes them feel less overwhelming.

7. Remind yourself to let go, kindly

A simple phrase can help, like “That chapter is closed” or “I'm allowed to move forward.” Repeat it when the loop starts. Over time, the reminder becomes automatic.

Tip: Keep a short note on your phone titled “Why it ended.” When you feel the urge to text them or romanticize the past, read it before you do anything else.

Eliminate reminders of your ex

8. Clear your space

Photos on the fridge, their hoodie on your chair, gifts on your shelf: every item is a cue. Pack them in a box and store them out of sight, or return things that belong to them through a friend.

9. Stop checking up on them

Every profile visit restarts the cycle. Mute, unfollow or block, whichever you need. If you share friends, ask them not to pass along updates for a while. Not knowing what your ex is doing is one of the fastest ways to stop thinking about it.

10. Update your daily routine

If your mornings involved texting them or your weekends were built around them, those time slots will feel empty and invite rumination. Fill them on purpose: a new morning walk, a Saturday class, a different coffee spot.

Focus on your future instead

11. Put your attention into something absorbing

Activities that require concentration, like learning an instrument, training for a race, a creative project or a challenging work goal, give your mind something else to chew on. For ideas, see our list of things to do to move on from a breakup.

12. Think about the life you want next

Write down what you want the next year to look like: career, friendships, travel, health. Imagining a future that excites you naturally pulls attention away from the past.

13. Take care of yourself

Sleep, movement, real meals and time outside sound basic, but heartbreak drains you, and a tired brain ruminates more. Treat this season as recovery. Our guide on how to be happy with yourself offers more ways to rebuild.

14. Open up to new love when you're ready

There is no deadline. You are ready when you can be curious about someone new without measuring them against your ex or using them to fill a hole. When that day comes, dating can be a joyful reminder of how much is still ahead.

Handling the hardest moments

Certain situations are almost guaranteed to bring your ex back to mind. Planning for them in advance takes away some of their power.

  • Birthdays, anniversaries and holidays. Fill the date with plans you look forward to, ideally with people who know it might be a tough day.
  • Hearing they are dating someone new. It will probably sting, even if you ended things. Let yourself feel it, then remind yourself that their timeline says nothing about your worth.
  • Running into them. Have a simple script ready, like “Hey, good to see you. I have to run,” and leave when you need to.
  • Late nights and weekends. Loneliness peaks when your schedule is empty. Line up a call, a show or an early-morning plan so you are not left alone with your thoughts.
  • Finding an old photo or message. Pause, breathe and put it away. You do not have to read the whole thread.

Each time you get through one of these moments without reaching out or spiraling, you strengthen the habit of letting go. It gets easier with practice. For a broader plan, see how to forget someone.

Mistakes that keep you stuck

  • Late-night texting “for closure.” These conversations usually reopen the wound.
  • Staying friends too soon. Friendship right after a breakup keeps hope alive.
  • Rebound relationships to avoid feelings. They often delay healing rather than speed it up.
  • Analyzing every detail with every friend. Talking helps; endless dissecting can keep you looping.
  • Judging yourself for still caring. Shame adds a second layer of pain. Caring means you loved; it will soften.

How long until you stop thinking about them?

There is no universal timeline. It depends on how long you were together, how it ended and what support you have. What matters is the direction: are the thoughts becoming less frequent and less painful over weeks and months? If yes, you are healing, even on days it does not feel like it. If you feel stuck or hopeless for a long stretch, reach out to a therapist.

The bottom line

You stop thinking about your ex not by forcing them out of your mind but by processing the loss, cutting the cues that keep pulling you back and building a present that is more interesting than the past. Be patient and kind with yourself. For more support, read how to move on after a breakup and how to get over a broken heart.
takeaways: Constant thoughts about an ex are a normal adjustment, not a personal failing.
Redirect thoughts instead of suppressing them, and try a daily time limit for rumination.
Remove reminders, stop checking their profiles and refresh your routine.
Focus on absorbing activities and the future you want; date again when you're truly ready.

faq.q: Why do I keep thinking about my ex?
faq.a: Your ex was woven into your routines, plans and identity, so your brain keeps reaching for that familiar connection. Unanswered questions about why it ended also keep the mind looping. Removing reminders, filling old routines with new activities and processing your feelings all help the thoughts fade.

faq.q: Is it normal to think about your ex every day?
faq.a: Yes, especially in the first weeks or months after a breakup. What matters is whether the thoughts are gradually becoming less frequent and less painful. If they are not easing over time, or they interfere with daily life, talking to a licensed therapist can help.

faq.q: Does no contact help you stop thinking about your ex?
faq.a: For most people, yes. Each text, call or profile visit restarts the emotional loop. A period of no contact gives your brain space to adjust. If you must stay in touch for kids or work, keep conversations brief, practical and neutral.

faq.q: How do I stop thinking about my ex at night?
faq.a: Create a calming wind-down routine, keep your phone out of reach, and write down any looping thoughts in a notebook before bed so they feel parked. Listening to a podcast or audiobook can give your mind something else to follow. Regular sleep and exercise also reduce rumination.
